content: Cesarean delivery on maternal request (CDMR) refers to an elective cesarean section performed not due to medical necessity or obstetrical indications but solely based on the pregnant patient’s request. Over the past century, cesarean sections (CS) have become increasingly safe, which has led to a broadening of the indications for their use. This shift has contributed to the growing acceptance of performing cesarean deliveries upon maternal request. It is estimated that 4-18% of all cesarean sections are performed at the request of the mother, though obtaining accurate estimates remains challenging. The movement advocating for CDMR may have originated in Brazil. The ethical principle that a woman has the right to make decisions about her own body has empowered women to choose their preferred method of childbirth. Additionally, as women live longer, concerns about potential damage to pelvic floor structures from vaginal delivery have added complexity to the discussion. Such damage can result in relaxation of the ligaments supporting the pelvic organs, potentially leading to urinary incontinence. This risk has become a significant consideration for some women. For women with an extreme fear of childbirth (tokophobia), undergoing a cesarean section raises the question of whether it constitutes a medical indication or simply a CDMR. In March 2006, a panel of experts convened by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) sought to address the medical issues surrounding CDMR. However, they concluded that there was insufficient evidence to fully evaluate the benefits and risks of CDMR compared to vaginal delivery. As a result, they were unable to reach a consensus on the general advisability of cesarean delivery by maternal request. Proponents of CDMR argue that it allows for a controlled and scheduled birth process, often with less bleeding and reduced risk of trauma to the baby. There is also some evidence suggesting that urinary stress incontinence, a long-term consequence of pelvic floor damage, is more common after vaginal delivery. However, this is often attributed to improper pushing techniques (e.g., directed pushing while lying on the back) rather than childbirth itself. When women are allowed to push in upright positions, the risk of stress incontinence is typically reduced. Opponents of elective cesarean sections (ECS) argue that the procedure is not natural, incurs higher costs, has higher infection rates, requires longer hospital stays, and is associated with lower breastfeeding rates. Additionally, once a cesarean section has been performed, subsequent deliveries are likely to also be cesarean sections, each carrying progressively higher risks. Furthermore, babies born via vaginal delivery tend to have a lower risk of infant respiratory distress syndrome compared to those born via cesarean section (77 vs. 62 per 1,000 live births). Researchers propose that the compression of the fetal lungs during vaginal delivery may play a beneficial role in the baby’s subsequent respiratory health, a process absent in cesarean deliveries. A study published in the February 13, 2007, issue of the Canadian Medical Association Journal found that women who had planned cesarean deliveries experienced a rate of severe complications more than three times higher than those who planned vaginal deliveries.
